The '''Herb and Chemical Atlas''' is the one-page index to everything in this library about plants, the chemicals in them, what those chemicals do to each other inside a person, and what people make out of them — cooking first, then lotions and balms, then diffusers and candles. Every entry here is a short line. The detail lives on the page each line links to.

It exists because the same plant turns up in four different conversations — a kitchen spice, a scent, a dye, and a drug interaction — and nowhere were those four facts on one line next to each other. Cooking is the centre of this page because cooking is where almost everyone meets these plants first.

== The charts ==
Two diagrams carry the structural part of this page. Both are drawn from the data files beside this article rather than copied from anywhere, so they are the same on every load and correct in print.

[[Figure:allylbenzene-map|The allylbenzene series, each ring position colour-coded. Two molecules can be compared by eye: what is at position 4 decides the class, position 2 and 5 are said to shift the character.]]

The colour key is the one from the chart the operator has used since 2018, published on Herbpedia: position 1 black (the side chain), 2 brown, 3 red, 4 green, 5 blue, 6 purple. '''What each position is said to do is a community claim''', from the 69Ron material, and is not a verified structure–activity result. It is on the chart because it is how this family has been read for twenty years, not because it has been demonstrated.

[[Figure:plant-constituents|What is in each plant: the major constituents of each essential oil, as a share of the whole. Bars are the midpoint of the published range.]]

Read that chart with one thing in mind: '''it is the composition of the oil, not of the plant.''' Piperine is 5–9% of black pepper but almost none of its distilled oil; curcumin is the colour and the pharmacology of turmeric and is not volatile at all; the grapefruit furanocoumarins that cause the famous drug interaction are in the juice, not the peel oil. A plant and its essential oil are not interchangeable, and most bad advice in this subject comes from treating them as if they were.

== Shulgin's ten essential oils ==
Shulgin noticed that ten common essential oils carry the ring substitution patterns of ten known amphetamines, and that adding ammonia across the side chain would, on paper, turn each oil into its partner. His own words are "in theory" and "in principle", and that qualifier is the whole point: '''no human in vivo conversion of an allylbenzene into an amphetamine has ever been demonstrated.''' Every pair below is hypothetical.

'''What is actually documented is different.''' Allylbenzenes fed to animals yield tertiary aminopropiophenone alkaloids - dimethylamine, piperidine and pyrrolidine types - detected in urine by GLC/CIMS, NOT amphetamines (Peele & Oswald, PMID 870079). Propenylbenzenes (anethole, alpha/beta-asarone, isoeugenol, isosafrole) form no such alkaloid metabolites at all. The only amphetamine-adjacent experimental claim in the series is the rabbit-liver myristicin to MMDA report Shulgin himself cites, and the repo's own knowledge file concedes the products were most likely aminopropiophenones.

The pairs, each one hypothetical:
* '''4-methoxy''' — estragole (methyl chavicol, 4-allylanisole) → 4-MA, 4-methoxyamphetamine
* '''3,4-dimethoxy''' — methyleugenol → 3,4-DMA, 3,4-dimethoxyamphetamine
* '''3,4-methylenedioxy''' — safrole → MDA, 3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine
* '''3-methoxy-4,5-methylenedioxy''' — myristicin → MMDA, 3-methoxy-4,5-methylenedioxyamphetamine
* '''2-methoxy-3,4-methylenedioxy''' — croweacin → MMDA-3a, 2-methoxy-3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine
* '''2-methoxy-4,5-methylenedioxy''' — asaricin → MMDA-2, 2-methoxy-4,5-methylenedioxyamphetamine
* '''3,4,5-trimethoxy''' — elemicin → TMA, 3,4,5-trimethoxyamphetamine
* '''2,4,5-trimethoxy''' — asarone → TMA-2, 2,4,5-trimethoxyamphetamine. Shulgin names 'asarone'. The common calamus isomers alpha- and beta-asarone are PROPENYL and form no alkaloid metabolites; only the rare ALLYL isomer gamma-asarone (euasarone, sekishone) fits the series.
* '''2,5-dimethoxy-3,4-methylenedioxy''' — apiole → DMMDA, 2,5-dimethoxy-3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine
* '''2,3-dimethoxy-4,5-methylenedioxy''' — dillapiole → DMMDA-2, 2,3-dimethoxy-4,5-methylenedioxyamphetamine
* '''2,3,4,5-tetramethoxy''' — 2,3,4,5-tetramethoxyallylbenzene → TA, 2,3,4,5-tetramethoxyamphetamine

See [[Shulgin Ten Essential Oils]], [[Shulgin Ten Essential Amphetamines and Metabolic Chemistry]] and [[Oilahuasca]].

''Comedogenic numbers come from the rabbit-ear assay (Kligman/Fulton era, e.g. Fulton 1989 J Soc Cosmet Chem 40:321-333; Fulton 1984 J Am Acad Dermatol PMID 6229554). The rabbit ear over-predicts human comedogenicity, tested many materials neat or at 10% in propylene glycol, and popular 0-5 lists online frequently cite no source at all. Treat as a weak hint; a finished formula must be judged on its own.''

== The plants ==
157 of them. Each line gives the major constituents, why a kitchen uses it, what it dyes, and what should stop you. The full record — chemotypes, enzyme targets, traditional and evidence-based medical use, interactions, regulatory status and sources — is in <code>knowledge/herb-atlas/plants.json</code>.

A warning that applies to every percentage on this page: '''these are indicative ranges, not assay values.''' Chemotype, cultivar, ploidy, growing conditions and distillation all move them, sometimes by an order of magnitude. Calamus makes the point: the usual rule of thumb is that the North American diploid carries little or no β-asarone while Asian material carries a great deal, but measured Himalayan ''diploid'' populations have come in at 7.4% and 11.7%, and a twenty-accession study found no relationship to ploidy at all. '''Treat unanalysed material as the hazardous type.'''

=== Culinary spice ===
* '''Ajwain''' — ''Trachyspermum ammi (L.) Sprague''; mainly thymol 35-60, gamma-terpinene 15-30, p-cymene 15-25; Thymol's sharp phenolic taste cuts heavy fried batters and legumes; it is added to gram-flour batters and breads explicitly for digestibility. Small…; Thymol irritant; large oral doses nausea. Omum water in infants is traditional; concentrated oil unsafe for infants.
* '''Allspice (pimento)''' — ''Pimenta dioica (L.) Merr.''; mainly eugenol 60-80, methyleugenol 2-12, beta-caryophyllene 3-10; Allspice is the economical single-spice shortcut because its eugenol-dominant oil overlaps clove, its methyleugenol adds the nutmeg-ish note and its…; dyes brown; Culinary use is benign. The oil carries both eugenol (hepatotoxic in overdose by the glutathione-depletion mechanism)…
* '''Anise (aniseed)''' — ''Pimpinella anisum L.''; mainly (E)-anethole 80-95, estragole (methyl chavicol) 0.5-5, anisaldehyde 0.1-3; Anethole has an extremely low odour threshold and reads as sweetness on the palate, so a small quantity makes a low-sugar baked good taste sweeter —…; Low at culinary and tea doses. EMA restricts the medicinal product to adults and adolescents over 12 and to no more…
* '''Annatto (achiote)''' — ''Bixa orellana L.''; mainly ishwarane major sesquiterpene, β-humulene / germacrene variable; Bixin is fat-soluble: seeds are fried gently in oil or lard to make achiote oil; norbixin (alkaline-extracted) colours water-based foods like cheese…; dyes orange to salmon-pink; yellow-orange on cotton; Low. JECFA ADI bixin 0-12 mg/kg bw, norbixin 0-0.6 mg/kg bw (unverified).
* '''Asafoetida''' — ''Ferula assa-foetida L. (also F. foetida, F. narthex)''; mainly (E)-1-propenyl sec-butyl disulfide 20-60, (Z)-1-propenyl sec-butyl disulfide 5-25, di-sec-butyl trisulfide 2-10; Its volatile disulfides mimic onion/garlic flavour, so it replaces alliums where those are avoided (Jain, some Vaishnava). * '''Black cardamom''' — ''Amomum subulatum Roxb.''; mainly 1,8-cineole 60-75, alpha-terpineol 3-8, beta-pinene 3-7; Cineole gives cooling lift to rich meat dishes; the fire-drying adds guaiacol smokiness that reads as savoury/meaty. Used whole in long braises where…; Low.

The real hazard is adulteration: 'Mexican vanilla' sold cheaply has repeatedly been found to be…

== Cooking ==
Cooking is where the chemistry on this page was worked out long before anyone named it. Four rules carry most of it.

* '''Most of what you are after is not water-soluble.''' The aroma compounds in the chart above are oils. That is why a spice blooms in hot fat and not in a watery sauce, why tempering — tadka, the Indian technique of frying whole spices in ghee and pouring it over the dish — extracts more in thirty seconds than an hour of simmering, and why an infused oil tastes of the herb while an infused broth often does not.
* '''Heat both makes and destroys flavour.''' Toasting builds new compounds through the Maillard reaction and the breakdown of sugars; it also drives off the volatile ones that were already there. This is the whole reason whole spices go in early and ground spices go in late, and why delicate herbs — basil, coriander leaf, dill — are added off the heat.
* '''Spice use tracks climate, and the usual explanation is antimicrobial.''' Billing and Sherman's 1998 survey across thousands of traditional recipes found hotter climates use more spices, and the most-used spices are the most strongly antibacterial. It is a correlation with a plausible mechanism rather than a proven cause, and it is often overstated — but the pattern is real and it is why the preserving traditions and the flavouring traditions are the same traditions.
* '''Pairings are not arbitrary.''' Shared aroma compounds explain a good deal of why certain things go together, and also why the rule inverts by cuisine — Western pairings tend to share compounds, East Asian pairings tend not to (Ahn and colleagues, 2011).

'''Infused oils, honeys and vinegars carry a real safety rule.''' Fresh plant material in oil, garlic above all, is a botulism risk: oil excludes air, the plant brings the spores and the water, and nothing in the jar stops them. Use dried material, or acidify, keep it refrigerated and use it inside a week. See [[Sauce Food Safety Acidification pH Garlic in Oil and Refrigeration]] and [[Tinctures Glycerites Syrups and Infused Oils and Butters]].

More: [[Cooking with Herbs and Spices]] · [[Scratch Cooking and Culinary Ratios]] · [[Cooking Methods]] · [[Preservation Fermentation and Spice]] · [[Traditional Spiced Formulations and Synergistic Blends]]

== Lotions, balms and salves ==
A balm is anhydrous — oil, butter and wax, no water. A lotion or cream has water in it, and the moment there is water there is something living in it within days.

* '''Balm ratio.''' Roughly 1 part wax to 4 parts oil by weight gives a soft salve; 1 to 3 gives a firm stick; 1 to 6 or 8 gives something barely set. Butters sit between: they add body without the brittleness wax gives. Test a spoonful in the freezer for two minutes rather than guessing at the whole batch.
* '''Anything with water needs a real preservative.''' Vitamin E is an antioxidant — it slows oils going rancid and does nothing whatever to bacteria or mould. A broad-spectrum preservative at its stated use rate and within its stated pH range is not optional in a water-containing product, and "natural" alternatives marketed as preservatives are mostly not.
* '''Essential oils have dermal limits, and they are lower than people expect.''' Around 1% for a leave-on body product is a common working figure — about 6 drops in 30 ml — and lower on the face, lower again for children, with several oils restricted much further. Cinnamon bark, oakmoss and isoeugenol are sensitisers; expressed citrus oils are phototoxic and have bergapten limits for leave-on use. Tisserand and Young is the reference that actually gives per-oil numbers.
* '''Infusing the oil.''' Dry plant material only, unless you intend to use it immediately and refrigerate it — the same water rule as the kitchen, for the same reason.

More: [[Tinctures Glycerites Syrups and Infused Oils and Butters]] · [[Soap Calculator]]

== Diffusers, candles and the air ==
* '''Diffusers.''' A few drops in 100 ml of water is a normal strength in an ultrasonic unit, run in short sessions rather than continuously. Intermittent is both more effective and safer: the nose stops registering a constant smell within minutes, so running it all day mostly just raises the dose.
* '''Cats are the serious exception.''' Cats lack much of the glucuronidation capacity other mammals use to clear phenols and terpenes, so oils that are unremarkable to a person accumulate in them. Tea tree is the best-documented harm. Birds are more sensitive still, by way of how their lungs work. A diffuser in a shared room is a dose for everyone in it, including the ones who cannot leave.
* '''Terpenes react with indoor ozone.''' Limonene and the pinenes in particular react to form formaldehyde and fine secondary aerosol. It is not a reason to avoid them; it is a reason to ventilate rather than to seal a room and run a diffuser into it.
* '''Candles.''' Fragrance load is typically 6–10% by weight of wax and is capped by what the wax will actually hold; above that it sweats out or pools. Soy is usually scented around 85 °C so the fragrance binds rather than flashing off. Wick size has to be tested against the actual vessel diameter, and a cured candle — a week or two — throws noticeably better than a fresh one. Essential oils have flash points, which matters for both the pour and the burn.

== Potentiation and drug interactions ==
This is the part of the page that can actually hurt someone. "Potentiation" and "drug interaction" are the same mechanism described by someone who wants the effect and by someone who doesn't — a plant that makes a drug stronger does it by blocking the enzyme that clears it, and the enzyme does not know which outcome was intended.

Most of these run through the cytochrome P450 enzymes, which metabolise the majority of drugs. '''Inhibit one and everything it clears rises in the blood; induce one and everything it clears falls''' — including the drug somebody depends on.

The ones that put people in hospital:
* '''MAOIs with tyramine-rich food''' — aged cheese, cured meat, soy sauce, miso, yeast extract, unpasteurised beer. Monoamine oxidase in the gut and liver normally destroys dietary tyramine; blocked, it reaches the circulation and can cause a hypertensive crisis. This applies to the β-carbolines in ayahuasca and Syrian rue as much as to prescription MAOIs.
* '''MAOIs with serotonergic drugs''' — SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, triptans, dextromethorphan. Serotonin syndrome. This is the single most dangerous combination in this whole subject, and the overlap between people taking an antidepressant and people interested in harmala alkaloids is not small.
* '''Grapefruit with CYP3A4 substrates''' — the furanocoumarins irreversibly disable intestinal CYP3A4, so the enzyme has to be rebuilt. The effect lasts far beyond the glass of juice, and for some drugs the resulting blood level is several times intended.
* '''St John's wort''' — the opposite problem. It induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, dropping the levels of immunosuppressants, antiretrovirals, anticoagulants and hormonal contraceptives, with pregnancies and transplant rejections in the literature.
* '''Kava with alcohol or other hepatotoxins''', against the background of the kava hepatotoxicity signal that took it off several markets.
* '''Nutmeg in quantity''' is genuinely toxic — prolonged, unpleasant and occasionally hospitalising — and the dose is the kind of amount a recipe would never call for.

Quieter but real: piperine from black pepper raises the absorption of many drugs and supplements by inhibiting CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, which is exactly why it is added to turmeric products; licorice can drive potassium down; ginkgo and garlic are discussed with anticoagulants; cassia carries enough coumarin to have a tolerable daily intake set for it; and caffeine is cleared by CYP1A2, so CYP1A2 inhibitors leave it in circulation much longer.

See [[Enzyme Inhibition Kinetics and Molecular Transporters]] and [[Kava Potentiation]].

=== The documented list ===
90 of them, each with its mechanism rather than a yes or no. The full records — evidence grade and the PubMed id for every claim — are in <code>knowledge/herb-atlas/applications.json</code>.

=== Major ===
* '''grapefruit juice (furanocoumarins: bergamottin, 6',7'-dihydroxybergamottin) + felodipine''' — Mechanism-based (irreversible) inactivation of intestinal (enterocyte) CYP3A4 by furanocoumarins; hepatic CYP3A4 largely spared. Effect lasts ~24-72 h until new enzyme is synthesized. Raises felodipine exposure (mean bioavailability 284% of water, range 164-469%); lower diastolic BP, higher heart rate. Nifedipine only 134%. (PMID 1671113, 23184849)
* '''grapefruit juice + simvastatin + lovastatin''' — Intestinal CYP3A4 inactivation; simvastatin/lovastatin have very high first-pass CYP3A4 extraction, so the effect is large. Raises statin and active acid exposure: double-strength juice 200 mL tid -> simvastatin Cmax ~9-fold, AUC far higher; lovastatin ~15-fold; one… (PMID 9834039, 9585793)
* '''grapefruit juice + cyclosporine (ciclosporin)''' — Intestinal CYP3A4 inactivation plus possible intestinal P-gp effects. Raises oral cyclosporine AUC (~55%) and Cmax (~35%); IV cyclosporine unaffected. (PMID 7768070, 7715295)
* '''Seville (bitter) orange juice + pomelo + CYP3A4 substrates (felodipine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus)''' — Same furanocoumarins (bergamottin, 6',7'-DHB) inactivate intestinal CYP3A4; pomelo also inhibits P-gp in vitro. Seville orange raised felodipine AUC 76% (grapefruit 93% in same study). Pomelo raised cyclosporine AUC/Cmax (~19%/12%) and caused a clinically… (PMID 11180034, 16513449)
* '''St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum; hyperforin) + cyclosporine''' — Hyperforin activates PXR -> induction of intestinal/hepatic CYP3A4 and intestinal P-gp (MDR1). Lowers cyclosporine levels (profound trough drops); acute rejection reported. (PMID 10683008, 10852634)
* '''St John's wort + combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol + norethindrone)''' — CYP3A4 induction (PXR) increases clearance of both estrogen and progestin. Lowers contraceptive exposure: increased norethindrone oral clearance, shorter ethinyl estradiol half-life; increased breakthrough bleeding and… (PMID 14663455, 15914127)
* '''St John's wort + indinavir''' — CYP3A4 (+P-gp) induction. Lowers indinavir AUC ~57% and trough ~81% in healthy volunteers - risk of HIV treatment failure and resistance. (PMID 10683007)
* '''St John's wort + digoxin''' — Induction of intestinal P-glycoprotein (MDR1) -> reduced absorption (digoxin is a P-gp probe, not CYP-metabolized). Lowers digoxin AUC ~25% and troughs ~33% after 10 days. (PMID 10546917, 11180019)
* '''St John's wort + SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine), nefazodone, other serotonergic drugs''' — Pharmacodynamic: hyperforin inhibits reuptake of serotonin (and other monoamines) -> additive serotonergic activity. Additive effect -> serotonin syndrome (agitation, tremor, clonus, hyperthermia). (PMID 10447148, 15784664)
* '''St John's wort + warfarin''' — Induction of CYP2C9 (S-warfarin) and CYP3A4/1A2 (R-warfarin). Lowers warfarin exposure: S-warfarin clearance rose from ~198 to ~270 mL/h; reduced INR / anticoagulant effect. Swedish reports of falling INR. (PMID 15089812, 10683030)
* '''goldenseal (Hydrastis canadensis; berberine, hydrastine) + CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 substrates''' — Inhibition (partly mechanism-based, methylenedioxyphenyl alkaloids) of CYP2D6 and CYP3A4/5. Raises exposure of CYP2D6 substrates (debrisoquine ratio ~40% inhibition) and CYP3A substrates (midazolam ~40% inhibition; midazolam AUC up in later… (PMID 15900287, 18214849)
* '''MAO inhibitors (irreversible: phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid) + tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured/fermented meats, tap beer, soy/fermented products, spoiled food)''' — Inhibition of gut/liver MAO-A removes first-pass metabolism of dietary tyramine; tyramine displaces noradrenaline from nerve terminals -> pressor response. Additive/pressor effect: hypertensive crisis (occipital headache, stroke risk). (PMID 14275713, 6034391)
* '''MAO inhibitors + SSRIs / SNRIs / clomipramine / tramadol / meperidine (pethidine) / dextromethorphan / methadone / tapentadol''' — Pharmacodynamic: MAO inhibition + serotonin reuptake inhibition -> massive synaptic serotonin (5-HT2A/1A over-stimulation). Additive/synergistic -> severe serotonin toxicity (hyperthermia, clonus, rigidity, death). (PMID 15784664, 16051647)
* '''harmala alkaloids (harmine, harmaline, tetrahydroharmine; Peganum harmala seeds, Banisteriopsis caapi/ayahuasca) + SSRIs and other serotonin reuptake inhibitors''' — Harmine/harmaline are potent reversible MAO-A inhibitors (RIMA-like); THH also weakly inhibits serotonin reuptake. Combined with an SSRI -> serotonin toxicity mechanism as for MAOI+SSRI… Additive/synergistic serotonergic effect -> serotonin syndrome. (PMID 9924842, 10404423)
* '''harmala alkaloids / ayahuasca (or any MAO-A inhibitor) + MDMA, amphetamine, methamphetamine, other releasers''' — MAO-A inhibition prevents breakdown of serotonin/noradrenaline released by MDMA/amphetamines -> massive monoamine excess. Synergistic -> serotonin toxicity, hyperthermia, hypertensive crisis; fatalities with MDMA + moclobemide. (PMID 12603236, 21570786)
* '''kava + liver (hepatotoxicity debate)''' — Idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity; proposed contributors: poor-quality raw material (aerial parts/peelings containing pipermethystine, mould/aflatoxin), acetone/ethanol extracts vs water… Adverse effect (hepatitis, rare liver failure/transplant). (PMID 20720265, 12821045)
* '''nutmeg (Myristica fragrans; myristicin, elemicin, safrole) + toxicity (alone; plus serotonergic/anticholinergic co-ingestions)''' — Myristicin/elemicin: anticholinergic-like and psychoactive effects; myristicin is a weak MAO inhibitor in vitro and is metabolised (CYP) to amphetamine-like derivatives (debated). Toxic effect: tachycardia, agitation, hallucinations, nausea, dry mouth, prolonged (24-48 h) intoxication. (PMID 24452991)
* '''licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra; glycyrrhizin -> glycyrrhetinic acid) + thiazide/loop diuretics, corticosteroids, laxatives''' — Glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits renal 11beta-HSD2 -> cortisol activates mineralocorticoid receptors (apparent mineralocorticoid excess/pseudohyperaldosteronism). Additive potassium loss with K-wasting diuretics -> hypokalaemia, hypertension, metabolic alkalosis, rhabdomyolysis/paralysis, arrhythmia; also… (PMID 2889032, 11751713)
* '''licorice + digoxin / digitalis glycosides''' — Indirect pharmacodynamic: licorice-induced hypokalaemia increases myocardial sensitivity to digoxin (enhanced Na+/K+-ATPase binding). Additive -> digoxin toxicity (arrhythmia) at otherwise 'therapeutic' digoxin levels. (PMID 2889032)
* '''garlic supplements + saquinavir''' — Induction of intestinal CYP3A4 and/or P-gp (exact mechanism unclear). Lowers saquinavir AUC ~51%, trough ~49%, Cmax ~54%; only partially recovered (60-70% of baseline) after 10-day washout. (PMID 11740713)
* '''cannabidiol (CBD) + clobazam''' — CBD inhibits CYP2C19 (and CYP3A4), blocking clearance of the active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam (nCLB, cleared by CYP2C19). Raises clobazam levels (~60%) and N-desmethylclobazam markedly (~500%) at 4 weeks, causing sedation; clobazam dose reduced in 77% of children. (PMID 26114620)
* '''cannabidiol (CBD) + warfarin''' — CBD inhibits CYP2C9 (S-warfarin) and CYP3A4. Raises warfarin effect (INR rose as CBD dose was escalated; warfarin dose had to be reduced ~30%). (PMID 29387536)
* '''cannabidiol (Epidiolex) + valproate (and clobazam)''' — Pharmacodynamic/hepatotoxic synergy, not a PK change (valproate levels are not raised); mechanism unclear (mitochondrial/hepatocellular stress). Additive hepatotoxicity: transaminase (ALT/AST) elevations >3x ULN occur predominantly in patients co-treated with valproate; risk also rises with… (PMID 28538134, 37458709)
* '''cannabis or tobacco SMOKE (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) + CYP1A2 substrates: clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline, caffeine''' — PAHs in smoke activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor -> CYP1A2 induction. Due to combustion products, not THC/CBD/nicotine. Smoking LOWERS clozapine/olanzapine levels; QUITTING (or switching to edibles/vaping/patches) RAISES levels by roughly 30-50%+ within 1-2 weeks ->… (PMID 11981356, 385272)
* '''green tea / green tea extract (EGCG, catechins) + nadolol; liver''' — Green tea catechins inhibit intestinal OATP1A2 uptake of nadolol. Separately, concentrated EGCG extracts cause idiosyncratic hepatocellular DILI, which is worse with fasting bolus dosing. Green tea LOWERS nadolol exposure (Cmax and AUC each down about 85%) and blunts its BP-lowering effect. Extracts raise the risk of liver injury. (PMID 24419562, 32140423)
* '''vitamin K1-rich leafy greens (kale, spinach, collards, chard, parsley, natto=K2) + warfarin''' — Pharmacodynamic: dietary vitamin K bypasses VKORC1 inhibition by supplying reduced vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X. Sudden increases lower INR (clot risk); sudden decreases raise INR (bleeding risk). (PMID 15121490, 27346552)
* '''yohimbe / yohimbine + MAOIs; hypertension/antihypertensives; stimulants''' — Alpha-2 adrenoceptor antagonist that increases central and peripheral noradrenaline release. With MAOIs or other sympathomimetics it adds to pressor load. Raises BP and HR, with risk of hypertensive crisis. Opposes clonidine and other antihypertensives. (PMID 11744068, 10337904)
* '''ephedra / ma huang (ephedrine alkaloids) + caffeine (and other stimulants)''' — Pharmacodynamic sympathomimetic synergy: ephedrine (indirect/direct adrenergic agonist) plus caffeine (adenosine antagonism, PDE inhibition). Additive/synergistic rises in BP, HR and arrhythmia risk. Reports of stroke, MI, seizure and sudden death. (PMID 11117974, 12672771)
* '''kratom (Mitragyna speciosa; mitragynine, 7-OH-mitragynine) + CYP3A substrates; CYP2D6 substrates; opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, other CNS depressants''' — PK: mitragynine strongly inhibits CYP2D6 and CYP3A in vitro. In humans kratom tea modestly inhibits intestinal CYP3A and has no measurable CYP2D6 effect. PD: mu-opioid partial agonism adds… Raises midazolam AUC 1.39x and Cmax 1.50x (CYP3A). Dextromethorphan (2D6) is unchanged. Additive CNS/respiratory depression with opioids and… (PMID 36924284, 30973850)
* '''Mucuna pruriens (natural L-DOPA) + MAOIs (nonselective: phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid; also linezolid)''' — L-DOPA is converted to dopamine and noradrenaline. With MAO-A blocked, catecholamine breakdown is prevented, leading to pressor crisis. Hypertensive crisis (raised BP, flushing, palpitations). (PMID 5451592, 15548480)
* '''5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan) + SSRIs/SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol; carbidopa''' — 5-HTP bypasses rate-limiting tryptophan hydroxylase and is decarboxylated to serotonin, adding to reuptake/MAO blockade (serotonin toxicity). Carbidopa inhibits peripheral AADC, raising… Additive serotonergic toxicity. Carbidopa raises 5-HTP exposure; the combination has been linked to scleroderma-like illness. (PMID 1918474, 4091416)
* '''L-tryptophan + MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine)''' — Precursor loading plus MAO-A blockade leads to excess serotonin. Serotonin toxicity (hyperreflexia, myoclonus, confusion, hyperthermia). (PMID 6691495, 3976924)
* '''berberine (goldenseal, barberry, Coptis, Oregon grape) + CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP3A4 substrates; cyclosporine''' — Inhibition of CYP2D6 (strongest), CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 after repeated dosing. Cyclosporine levels raised via CYP3A4 (and possibly P-gp). RAISES exposure of 2D6/2C9/3A4 substrates. Markedly raises cyclosporine blood concentrations. (PMID 21870106, 16133554)
* '''Schisandra (S. sphenanthera / Wuzhi tablet; S. chinensis) + tacrolimus (also other CYP3A/P-gp substrates)''' — Lignans (schisantherin A, deoxyschizandrin) inhibit intestinal/hepatic CYP3A and P-gp. RAISES tacrolimus exposure substantially (oral bioavailability up). (PMID 17506780, 24195812)
* '''calcium/dairy (milk, yogurt), antacids, iron, zinc, magnesium + tetracyclines; fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin)''' — Chelation of divalent/trivalent cations by the drug in the gut, forming non-absorbable complexes. LOWERS antibiotic absorption: milk/yogurt cut ciprofloxacin AUC by 30-36% and Cmax by 36-47%. Tetracycline loss is larger. (PMID 1934862, 946598)
* '''alcohol (chronic heavy use) / fasting + acetaminophen (paracetamol)''' — Chronic ethanol induces CYP2E1, increasing NAPQI formation, while depleting glutathione (malnutrition, fasting). Acute ethanol competitively inhibits CYP2E1 and is transiently protective. Increased hepatotoxicity at therapeutic-to-modestly-supratherapeutic acetaminophen doses in chronic drinkers. (PMID 7657281)
* '''alcohol + benzodiazepines; opioids (and gabapentinoids, Z-drugs)''' — Pharmacodynamic additive/synergistic CNS and respiratory depression (GABA-A potentiation + mu-opioid brainstem depression). Ethanol may also raise some benzodiazepine levels acutely… Synergistic respiratory depression, sedation and overdose death. (PMID 28170358, 11990206)
* '''alcohol + metformin; MAOIs (tap/draft beer tyramine)''' — Metformin: ethanol inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis and raises NADH/NAD+, increasing lactate production while reducing clearance, which adds to metformin's lactate burden (worse with… Metformin + binge alcohol raises lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia risk. MAOI + high-tyramine beer causes hypertensive crisis. (PMID 38983827, 41281028)
* '''black licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra; glycyrrhizin -> glycyrrhetinic acid) + spironolactone; ACE inhibitors/ARBs; thiazide/loop diuretics; digoxin''' — Glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits renal 11beta-HSD2, so cortisol occupies the mineralocorticoid receptor (apparent mineralocorticoid excess): Na/water retention, K loss, hypertension. Opposes the antihypertensive effect of ACEi/ARBs and diuretics. Additive hypokalaemia with thiazide/loop diuretics, which raises digoxin toxicity… (PMID 37764649, 31379750)
* '''sage (Salvia officinalis) oil, camphor, eucalyptus, hyssop, rosemary, pennyroyal essential oils (ingested) + seizure threshold; proconvulsant drugs; epilepsy''' — Monoterpene ketones (thujone, camphor) and 1,8-cineole are convulsant via GABA-A antagonism and other mechanisms. Seizures and status epilepticus after ingestion, especially in children. Additive with proconvulsant drugs. (PMID 22353306, 21907890)
* '''pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium / Hedeoma; pulegone) + liver; CYP inducers/inhibitors; acetaminophen; N-acetylcysteine (treatment)''' — Pulegone is bioactivated by CYP (CYP1A2, 2E1, 2C19) to menthofuran and reactive electrophiles that deplete glutathione, causing centrilobular hepatic necrosis (and renal toxicity). Hepatotoxicity. Theoretically worse with CYP inducers or GSH depletion (fasting, chronic alcohol, acetaminophen). NAC may be protective. (PMID 8633832, 28905185)
* '''topical methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen, sports rubs, Chinese medicated oils) + warfarin''' — Percutaneous salicylate absorption (large areas, occlusion, heat) potentiates warfarin, possibly via protein-binding displacement and hypoprothrombinaemic and antiplatelet salicylate… RAISES INR / bleeding, including life-threatening bleeding. (PMID 2371186, 10860133)
* '''eucalyptus oil (1,8-cineole) ingestion + children (also CNS depressants)''' — Direct CNS toxicity of cineole, plus aspiration pneumonitis. Dose-related CNS depression, ataxia, seizures, vomiting and aspiration. (PMID 7651249, 9270157)
* '''tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia; terpinen-4-ol) + ingestion (children, pets)''' — Terpene CNS toxicity and aspiration risk. Ataxia, drowsiness, confusion and CNS depression after ingestion of millilitre amounts. Topically: contact dermatitis from oxidised oil. (PMID 16243420, 12813303)

=== Moderate ===
* '''grapefruit juice + midazolam (oral) + triazolam''' — Intestinal CYP3A4 inactivation; only the oral route is affected. Raises oral midazolam AUC ~52%, Cmax ~56%, stronger sedation; IV midazolam unchanged. Raises triazolam concentrations (~48% AUC). (PMID 7628179, 7648762)
* '''goldenseal + metformin''' — Predicted from in vitro: inhibition of OCT1/2 and MATE1/2-K transporters. Observed in vivo: reduced absorption, mechanism not fully explained (possibly intestinal uptake/OCT3 or other). LOWERS metformin AUC (GMR ~0.77) and Cmax (~0.73); no change in half-life or renal clearance. Midazolam (CYP3A) AUC raised as positive control; no… (PMID 33174626)
* '''harmala alkaloids (reversible MAO-A inhibitors) + tyramine-rich foods''' — Reversible competitive MAO-A inhibition; high tyramine concentrations can partly displace a reversible inhibitor, so pressor potentiation is smaller than with irreversible MAOIs but not… Additive pressor effect (raised tyramine exposure) -> possible hypertensive reaction. (PMID 35600851, 30255284)
* '''kava (Piper methysticum; kavalactones) + alcohol (ethanol)''' — Pharmacodynamic additive CNS depression (kavalactones modulate GABA-A, block Na+/Ca2+ channels); possible additive hepatic stress. Additive: kava alone had little effect but kava + alcohol produced greater impairment on divided attention and subjective intoxication than alcohol… (PMID 16203421, 8481222)
* '''kava + benzodiazepines (alprazolam)''' — Pharmacodynamic additive GABAergic CNS depression; possible additional PK contribution (kavalactone CYP inhibition) not established. Additive sedation -> lethargic, disoriented semi-comatose state. (PMID 8967683)
* '''kava + CYP2E1 substrates (chlorzoxazone probe; also ethanol, acetaminophen metabolism)''' — Inhibition of CYP2E1. Raises CYP2E1 substrate exposure (~40% reduction in chlorzoxazone 6-hydroxylation ratio). Kava did NOT inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2D6 or CYP3A in vivo in… (PMID 15900287, 17495878)
* '''Ginkgo biloba + warfarin / antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel)''' — Proposed: ginkgolide B platelet-activating-factor antagonism (antiplatelet); no meaningful CYP2C9 effect. Controlled data: NO change in INR or S/R-warfarin PK, and no warfarin dose change needed in an RCT. Case reports: spontaneous bleeding (hyphema… (PMID 15801937, 12083489)
* '''turmeric / curcumin + tacrolimus; warfarin / vitamin K antagonists''' — Curcumin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp in vitro (raising tacrolimus); antiplatelet activity and possible CYP2C9 inhibition (warfarin). Raises tacrolimus levels (case of toxicity in renal transplant patient eating turmeric/curry); raised INR with vitamin K antagonist (case). (PMID 37586787, 25230280)
* '''piperine + phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline''' — Inhibition of CYP-mediated metabolism (CYP1A2, CYP3A4, CYP2C9) and P-gp; possibly increased absorption. Raises exposure: propranolol and theophylline AUC/Cmax increased after a single 20 mg piperine dose; phenytoin AUC/Cmax increased in volunteers and… (PMID 1815977, 11808866)
* '''piperine + CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein substrates (digoxin, cyclosporine, verapamil etc.)''' — Direct inhibition of human P-gp (Caco-2 digoxin/cyclosporine transport) and CYP3A4 (human liver microsomes; verapamil metabolism). Raises exposure (predicted) of dual CYP3A4/P-gp substrates; inhibition is mixed-type at low-micromolar concentrations. (PMID 12130727)
* '''chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla) + warfarin''' — Proposed: coumarin constituents (herniarin, umbelliferone) additive anticoagulant effect and/or CYP inhibition (in vitro CYP1A2/3A4) - mechanism unconfirmed. Raised INR and bleeding: 70-year-old woman on warfarin, INR ~7.9 with retroperitoneal and other haematomas after drinking chamomile tea (4-5… (PMID 16636327)
* '''Echinacea purpurea root + CYP3A substrates (midazolam), CYP1A2 substrates (caffeine), lopinavir/ritonavir''' — Mixed: inhibits intestinal CYP3A while inducing hepatic CYP3A; inhibits CYP1A2. Oral midazolam: net small change (intestinal inhibition offsets hepatic induction); IV midazolam clearance increased 34%, AUC down 23%; caffeine… (PMID 14749695, 20653355)
* '''fluvoxamine + caffeine''' — Potent CYP1A2 inhibition by fluvoxamine (also CYP2C19); caffeine is ~95% CYP1A2-cleared. Raises caffeine exposure: total clearance fell ~80% (107 -> 21 mL/min), half-life 5 -> 31 h. Even 10-20 mg/day fluvoxamine inhibits CYP1A2. (PMID 8807660, 11907488)
* '''ciprofloxacin (and enoxacin, more potent) + caffeine''' — Quinolone inhibition of CYP1A2-mediated caffeine N-demethylation. Raises caffeine exposure: clearance reduced (~30-50% with ciprofloxacin, dose-dependent; enoxacin much stronger), half-life prolonged. (PMID 2729942, 2589393)
* '''caffeine (coffee, tea, energy drinks) + clozapine''' — Competitive inhibition of CYP1A2 by caffeine (both are CYP1A2 substrates). Raises clozapine exposure: controlled study ~19% AUC increase (14% lower clearance) in healthy volunteers; in patients, removing caffeine from the… (PMID 10606838, 9690697)
* '''alcohol (ethanol) + common ink cap mushroom (Coprinopsis atramentaria, formerly Coprinus atramentarius; coprine)''' — Coprine is metabolised to 1-aminocyclopropanol, which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) -> acetaldehyde accumulation (disulfiram-like). Disulfiram-like reaction when alcohol is taken from ~30 min up to ~72 h after eating the mushroom: flushing, palpitations, tachycardia… (PMID 350009, 577107)
* '''alcohol (ethanol) + metronidazole (also tinidazole)''' — Traditionally claimed ALDH inhibition (disulfiram-like); controlled evidence does not support raised acetaldehyde. Alternative explanations: coincident adverse effects of either drug alone… Classic claim: flushing, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia. RCT: metronidazole did NOT raise blood acetaldehyde or cause objective/subjective reactions… (PMID 10676835, 12022894)
* '''cassia cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia/aromaticum) coumarin + liver''' — Coumarin hepatotoxicity in a susceptible subset of humans; coumarin cleared mainly by CYP2A6 7-hydroxylation, with the minor 3,4-epoxidation pathway producing hepatotoxic… Dose-dependent rise in liver-injury risk (reversible transaminase elevations) when intake exceeds the TDI. (PMID 20024932, 21462332)
* '''American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius); Asian ginseng (P. ginseng) + warfarin''' — Unclear; possible induction of warfarin metabolism or a pharmacodynamic effect. Ginsenosides also have in-vitro antiplatelet activity. LOWERS warfarin effect: INR and plasma warfarin both decreased vs placebo. (PMID 15238367)
* '''ginseng (Panax) + phenelzine (MAOI)''' — Unknown; possibly additive CNS stimulation or monoaminergic effects. Additive adverse effects: headache, insomnia, tremor, irritability/manic-like symptoms. (PMID 3597812)
* '''dong quai (Angelica sinensis) + warfarin''' — Unknown. Contains coumarin derivatives (e.g., osthole) and ferulic acid with antiplatelet activity. Rabbit data show a pharmacodynamic but not a pharmacokinetic effect. Raises INR / bleeding risk. (PMID 10417036, 7588995)
* '''fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) + warfarin''' — Proposed: coumarin-type constituents and antiplatelet effects. The mechanism is unproven. Raises INR (case with boldo+fenugreek, positive rechallenge). (PMID 11310527)
* '''ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) + liver; thyroid (levothyroxine, antithyroid drugs)''' — Idiosyncratic cholestatic/mixed DILI. Separately, it raises thyroid hormone (T4/T3), with case reports of thyrotoxicosis and painless thyroiditis. Liver injury after 2-12 week latency. May raise thyroid hormones, which adds to levothyroxine and opposes antithyroid therapy. (PMID 31991029, 35475098)
* '''valerian (Valeriana officinalis) + CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol, opioids, Z-drugs, barbiturates)''' — Pharmacodynamic GABAergic additivity (valerenic acid is a GABA-A modulator). Minimal CYP effect. Additive sedation/psychomotor impairment. No meaningful PK change for CYP3A4/2D6 substrates. (PMID 15328251, 19441067)
* '''hops (Humulus lupulus), passionflower (Passiflora incarnata) + sedatives/hypnotics, alcohol''' — Pharmacodynamic additive CNS depression (GABAergic; hops 2-methyl-3-buten-2-ol). Additive sedation. (PMID 19441067)
* '''bitter orange (Citrus aurantium; p-synephrine) + caffeine''' — p-Synephrine has weak alpha-1 and beta-3 adrenergic activity (much weaker than m-synephrine/phenylephrine or ephedrine). Pressor effects in products mainly come from caffeine and… In controlled trials p-synephrine up to ~100 mg did not augment the BP/HR effects of caffeine. Multi-ingredient 'ephedra-free' products raised BP/HR. (PMID 29047215, 16164886)
* '''betel nut / areca (arecoline) + antipsychotics + anticholinergics (procyclidine)''' — Pharmacodynamic: arecoline is a muscarinic agonist that antagonises anticholinergic anti-EPS drugs and adds cholinergic tone. Precipitates extrapyramidal symptoms (rigidity, tremor, akathisia) in patients on depot neuroleptics. (PMID 2572964)
* '''SAMe (S-adenosyl-L-methionine) + SSRIs/TCAs (clomipramine), MAOIs''' — SAMe is a methyl donor in monoamine synthesis and has antidepressant serotonergic effects, adding to serotonergic drugs. Serotonin toxicity (case with clomipramine). (PMID 8434674)
* '''resveratrol (high-dose supplements) + CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 substrates; CYP1A2 substrates''' — At 1 g/day for 4 weeks: inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and induces CYP1A2 (phenotyping cocktail). May raise exposure of 3A4/2D6/2C9 substrates and lower exposure of 1A2 substrates. (PMID 20716633)
* '''quercetin supplements + P-gp substrates (talinolol, digoxin?), CYP2C9 (diclofenac), CYP2E1 (chlorzoxazone)''' — Mixed: P-gp induction (Wang 2013) and OATP modulation lowering talinolol exposure. CYP2C9 and CYP2E1 inhibition in short human trials. Bidirectional and drug-specific: talinolol slightly LOWER, diclofenac and chlorzoxazone HIGHER. (PMID 24472704, 23422925)
* '''psyllium / high-fibre meals; also coffee, soy, calcium, iron + levothyroxine; also digoxin, lithium, carbamazepine, metformin (fibre binding)''' — Physical adsorption/binding in gut and delayed gastric emptying. Calcium/iron/aluminium chelate T4. May lower or delay absorption. (PMID 9737361, 33801406)
* '''grapefruit juice (naringin), also orange and apple juice + fexofenadine (OATP1A2 substrate)''' — Inhibition of intestinal OATP1A2 uptake transporter (not CYP3A). LOWERS fexofenadine exposure: AUC and Cmax reduced to about 30-40% of the water control. (PMID 11823753, 19789373)
* '''orange juice, apple juice + celiprolol; fexofenadine; aliskiren, atenolol, some others (OATP1A2/2B1 substrates)''' — Intestinal OATP inhibition by juice flavonoids (hesperidin, phloridzin). Possible pH/complexation contribution. LOWERS exposure: orange juice cut celiprolol AUC by about 83%. Apple and orange juice lower fexofenadine. (PMID 15001969, 11823753)
* '''wormwood (Artemisia absinthium) / absinthe; thujone + seizure-threshold-lowering drugs (bupropion, tramadol, tricyclics, some antipsychotics); epilepsy; anticonvulsants''' — alpha-Thujone is a noncompetitive GABA-A receptor antagonist (chloride-channel blocker). It is rapidly detoxified by CYP-mediated hydroxylation. Lowers seizure threshold, which adds to other proconvulsants and may oppose anticonvulsant control. (PMID 10725394, 15896935)
* '''tamarind (Tamarindus indica fruit) + aspirin''' — Unclear; likely enhanced absorption (acidic fruit pulp affecting dissolution/ionisation) plus reduced elimination. RAISES aspirin/salicylate bioavailability (salicylic acid AUC ~172 to ~266 mg/mL·h, about +55%; Cmax ~44 to ~68). (PMID 8980919)
* '''cruciferous vegetables (Brussels sprouts, cabbage, broccoli; indoles/sulforaphane); charcoal-broiled meat (PAHs) + CYP1A2 substrates (theophylline, caffeine, clozapine, olanzapine, tizanidine, phenacetin/antipyrine probes)''' — Aryl-hydrocarbon-receptor-mediated induction of CYP1A2 (PAHs from charbroiling; indole-3-carbinol products). Also induction of glucuronidation (cruciferous). LOWERS exposure of CYP1A2 substrates: faster phenacetin, antipyrine and theophylline clearance. Acetaminophen conjugation unaffected by charbroiled… (PMID 758247, 630792)

=== Minor ===
* '''garlic (Allium sativum; supplements/high dose) + warfarin''' — Proposed antiplatelet effect (ajoene, inhibits platelet aggregation) -> additive bleeding tendency; no consistent PK change. Case reports of raised INR/bleeding; aged garlic extract RCT showed no increased bleeding risk or INR change. (PMID 16484565, 17918162)
* '''piperine (black pepper) + curcumin''' — Inhibition of hepatic and intestinal glucuronidation (UGT) of curcumin, plus CYP3A4/P-gp inhibition. Raises curcumin bioavailability: in humans 2 g curcumin + 20 mg piperine increased bioavailability ~2000% (20-fold) with no adverse effects in that… (PMID 9619120)
* '''coumarin (cassia, tonka, sweet woodruff, melilot) + hepatotoxic drugs (acetaminophen, methotrexate, isoniazid, azoles, valproate, etc.)''' — Additive hepatotoxic load. People with low CYP2A6 activity (CYP2A6*4/*2 alleles, or CYP2A6 inhibitors such as methoxsalen or tranylcypromine) shunt more coumarin to the 3,4-epoxide pathway. Additive liver-injury risk; CYP2A6 inhibition raises the fraction going down the toxic pathway. (PMID 10418958, 20024932)
* '''green tea + warfarin''' — Vitamin K1 is present in dried tea leaf, plus possible antiplatelet catechin effects. Antagonism: lower INR, reported with very high intake. (PMID 10332534)
* '''cranberry juice/extract + warfarin''' — Proposed CYP2C9 inhibition is NOT supported in vivo. A possible minor pharmacodynamic effect (salicylic acid content, flavonoids). Possible small INR increase. Controlled trials show no PK change. (PMID 17392729, 19553405)
* '''pomegranate juice/extract + warfarin (CYP2C9 substrate)''' — In vitro CYP2C9 (and CYP3A) inhibition that did NOT translate to humans (no change in flurbiprofen clearance). Case reports describe raised INR while drinking and a subtherapeutic INR after stopping. The mechanism is unconfirmed. (PMID 23047652, 19637955)
* '''nutmeg / mace (myristicin, elemicin, safrole) + MAOIs / serotonergic drugs''' — Myristicin showed weak MAO inhibition in rodent tissue (1963). Clinical relevance is unestablished. Theoretical additive MAO inhibition or serotonergic effect. (PMID 13994372, 39559662)
* '''Rhodiola rosea + serotonergic drugs / MAOIs''' — In vitro MAO-A and MAO-B inhibition by root extracts. Theoretical additive serotonergic/MAO effect. (PMID 19168123)
* '''milk thistle (silymarin, silibinin) + CYP substrates (CYP1A2, 2D6, 2E1, 3A4)''' — In vitro CYP3A/2C9 and UGT inhibition. Human phenotyping shows no clinically relevant effect. No meaningful change for midazolam (3A), debrisoquine (2D6), caffeine (1A2) or chlorzoxazone (2E1). (PMID 15536458, 16432272)
* '''capsaicin (chili; topical capsaicin) + ACE inhibitors (cough); aspirin (absorption)''' — ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin and substance P and sensitise the TRPV1 cough reflex, so capsaicin triggers cough more easily. Ingested capsaicin alters GI mucosa and absorption (rat data). Cough induction with topical capsaicin in an ACEi patient (case). Lower salicylate bioavailability with chili in rats. (PMID 2221491, 10537230)
